opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a really formative period for me. Back then I was working on a project about automatic photo retouching, basically, given a raw-looking photo, can a machine learn to edit it the way a professional photographer would? The tricky part was that we didn't have paired data. You can't easily get the same photo before and after a pro edits it, at scale. So we framed the editing process as a sequence of operations, like adjusting exposure, contrast, white balance, saturation, and used reinforcement learning to decide which operation to apply next. And then we used a GAN-style discriminator to judge whether the result looked like it came from a collection of professionally edited photos.

What struck me was two things. First, it actually worked, sometimes surprisingly well. Seeing a network learn something that feels like taste or aesthetic judgment was kind of magical. And because the output was a sequence of interpretable filters rather than a black-box pixel output, you could see what it was "thinking," which I liked a lot.

But second, and maybe more importantly, it was really painful to train. GANs were unstable, RL was unstable, and combining the two was like stacking two unstable things on top of each other. You'd tweak a hyperparameter and everything would collapse. A lot of the time was spent babysitting training runs rather than thinking about the actual problem.

So my impression of AI from that experience was kind of mixed. On one hand, I was convinced these methods were powerful and would keep getting better. On the other hand, I felt that I personally enjoyed problems where you have more control, where you understand why something works. That pushed me back toward things like physical simulation and computer graphics, and eventually toward building tools and compilers like Taichi, where the goal is to make the computation itself more productive and predictable. In a way, the frustration with the tooling was part of what motivated me to care so much about infrastructure later on.

r001.rationale: The response says GAN and reinforcement learning training was unstable and frustrating, but it does not state that Hu concluded the technologies were not yet mature.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a pretty humbling experience, and it shaped how I think about AI even today.

This was back when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, around 2016 or 2017. I was fascinated by image post-processing, things like exposure adjustment, color grading, the kind of edits a professional retoucher does in Lightroom. And the question I had was, can we teach a machine to do this the way a human artist does, step by step, in a way that's actually understandable?

So the natural idea was to combine reinforcement learning with GANs. The reinforcement learning agent would pick a sequence of operations, like adjust exposure, then adjust contrast, then tweak the color curve. And the GAN discriminator would judge whether the result looked like a professionally retouched photo. On paper it's elegant. You get interpretable edits and you don't need paired data.

In practice, it was brutal. Both RL and GANs are notoriously unstable on their own, and when you put them together, the instability compounds. I spent months where the training would just collapse, or the agent would learn some degenerate policy like cranking saturation to the maximum because that fooled the discriminator for a while. The whole thing felt like balancing a pencil on its tip while riding a bicycle.

But two impressions came out of that. The first was that AI, at least at the time, was far less magical than the headlines suggested. Making it work was ninety percent engineering, debugging, and understanding your data and your reward signal. That demystified the field for me in a healthy way.

The second was more important for what I did later. I realized a huge amount of my time was not spent on the ideas but on the infrastructure. Writing custom operators, getting things to run efficiently on the GPU, making the differentiable image operations fast enough to iterate. The tools were really the bottleneck. And that frustration planted the seed that eventually became Taichi. I thought, if I'm going to spend most of my energy fighting tooling, maybe I should build better tooling so that researchers can spend their time on the actual problem.

So I'd say that project gave me respect for how hard AI is, and a conviction that the people building the underlying infrastructure matter just as much as the people designing the models.

r001.rationale: The response describes combined RL and GAN training as unstable and says AI felt less magical at the time, but it does not clearly state that this led Hu to regard those technologies as not yet mature.

astra-6.text: My early impression was that AI was very promising, but also difficult to control. I tried reinforcement learning and GANs for image post-processing, and getting something to work was much less straightforward than I expected. You could have an appealing idea, but turning it into a reliable result required a lot of experimentation. That made me excited about the possibilities, while also aware of the gap between an impressive demonstration and a tool you can consistently use.

r001.rationale: The response describes the work as difficult and says reliable results required experimentation, but it does not clearly state that GANs and reinforcement learning were not yet mature.

You could get interesting results, but making those results reliable was a different challenge. It made me curious about AI, while also making me aware of the gap between an impressive demonstration and a practical tool.
